igcse-0580-exponential-growth-decay-grow.description: Model a fixed percentage increase per time period and forecast a future amount using a power of the growth factor.

sections.title: Why does a multiplier become a power?
sections.label: Use a factor each period
sections.intro: A forecast may say that a quantity grows by a fixed percentage per year, per week or per other interval. Apply the percentage to the latest amount at the start of that interval.

blocks.html: From initial value \(A_0\), the model after \(k\) complete periods is \(A_k=A_0m^k\). For an increase of \(r\%\) per period, use \(m=1+\frac{r}{100}\).

figure.alt: Five dots rise from ten at interval zero to just above fifty after four intervals.
figure.caption: The dots show \(10\times1.5^k\) at complete intervals.

blocks.title: Forecast a population several years ahead
blocks.prompt: A town has \(7800\) residents at the beginning of the model. The population is modelled to grow by \(5.5\%\) each year. Estimate the population at the end of \(6\) years. Give your answer to the nearest hundred.
blocks.solution:
One year uses the multiplier \(1.055\).

\(7800\times1.055^{6}\approx10754.97\) before the final rounding.

To the nearest hundred, this is \(10800\) residents.
blocks.hint: Apply the same growth multiplier once per year, then round the final model value.

retry.feedback: The increase is a percentage of each year’s new population. Raise the multiplier to the number of years.

blocks.html: Adding the same amount each period is a different model. In exponential growth the same factor acts on a growing quantity.

blocks.title: Match the exponent to the time interval
blocks.prompt: A storage forecast starts with \(2200\) GB. The model increases this storage requirement by \(8\%\) every two weeks. Find the exact modelled requirement, in GB, after \(6\) weeks.
blocks.solution:
There are \(\frac{6}{2}=3\) complete two-week intervals.

The storage is multiplied by \(1.08\) once per interval.

\(2200\times1.08^{3}=2771.3664\) GB.
blocks.hint: Divide the number of weeks by two before choosing the exponent.

blocks.html: Count complete periods. If the rate applies every two weeks, two weeks represent one multiplication.

sections.title: What do the three parts of the equation tell me?
sections.label: Read an exponential model
sections.intro: The number outside the power gives the initial value. The base gives the change per period. The exponent says how many times that change has happened.

blocks.html: At \(k=0\), the factor is \(m^0=1\), so the value is the initial amount. An example is \(10\times1.5^k\), where each period has a \(50\%\) increase.

blocks.title: Read the growth rate from the factor
blocks.prompt: The forecast for a settlement is \(P(k)=10440\times1.082^k\), where \(k\) counts years since the start. Find the annual percentage increase in the model. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.solution:
The factor multiplying the population each year is \(1.082\).

The part in excess of 1 is \(1.082-1=0.082\).

The increase per year is \(8.2\%\).
blocks.hint: Subtract 1 from the multiplier before converting the growth part to a percentage.

retry.feedback: That is the new amount as a percentage of the old one. Subtract the original hundred percent to give the increase.

blocks.html: The exponent applies to the multiplier. If you put the initial amount and the multiplier in the brackets before taking a power, you also raise the initial amount.

blocks.title: Use the equation at an elapsed time
blocks.prompt: A garden’s forecast area, in square metres, is \(A(k)=16200\times1.032^k\), where \(k\) is the number of years after planting. Work out the area after \(5\) years to the nearest square metre.

field.label: Area to the nearest square metre

blocks.solution:
Substitute \(k=5\) and raise only the multiplier to this power.

\(16200\times1.032^{5}\approx18963\) square metres to the stated precision.
blocks.hint: Read the starting value and multiplier from the equation, then use the given year as the exponent.

blocks.html: A forecast is an estimate conditional on the assumed rate staying the same.

sections.title: How do I read the date and answer the quantity asked for?
sections.label: Use elapsed time and keep precision
sections.intro: The starting date is period zero. A question may ask for the complete forecast at a later date, or only the increase from the starting amount.

blocks.html: Subtract the dates to count elapsed years when comparing matching points in the year. For an increase in amount, subtract the initial amount from the modelled final amount.

blocks.title: Find the additional amount over several periods
blocks.prompt: Moisture in a prepared sample has starting mass \(1680\) g. For this test the model increases the mass by \(1.6\%\) each day. By how many grams does the modelled mass increase over \(3\) days? Give the exact increase.
blocks.solution:
Compute the final mass. \(1680\times1.016^{3}=1761.93712128\) g.

Subtract the starting mass to find the increase.

\(1761.93712128-1680=81.93712128\) g.
blocks.hint: Calculate the complete model value first. The question asks for the difference from the start.

retry.feedback: That is the final mass. Subtract the starting mass to get the increase.

blocks.html: Rounding the amount after each year changes the next year’s base and can shift the final answer.

blocks.title: Set the starting date to period zero
blocks.prompt: At the end of \(2031\), a seed library records \(880\) packets. It expects the stock to grow by \(16\%\) per year. Find the modelled number at the end of \(2034\), to the nearest packet.
blocks.solution:
The first date is period zero. The number of full years is \(2034-2031=3\).

\(880\times1.16^{3}\approx1374\) packets to the stated precision.
blocks.hint: Subtract the starting year from the later year. Do not count the starting endpoint as another period.

retry.feedback: The initial date is period zero. Count the elapsed years between the two dates.

blocks.html: Retain the unrounded result until the final line. Use the precision and unit in the question.

revision.body:
Methods

MethodWhat to do
Use a factor each periodFrom initial value \(A_0\), the model after \(k\) complete periods is \(A_k=A_0m^k\). For an increase of \(r\%\) per period, use \(m=1+\frac{r}{100}\).
Read an exponential modelAt \(k=0\), the factor is \(m^0=1\), so the value is the initial amount. An example is \(10\times1.5^k\), where each period has a \(50\%\) increase.
Use elapsed time and keep precisionSubtract the dates to count elapsed years when comparing matching points in the year. For an increase in amount, subtract the initial amount from the modelled final amount.

Worked line

\(240\times1.1^3=319.44\)

Check yourself

A reserve records \(640\) shrubs. The count model rises by \(25\%\) each year. Find the modelled count after two years.

Answer \(1000\) shrubs
revision.checks:
• Adding the same amount each period is a different model. In exponential growth the same factor acts on a growing quantity.
  • The exponent applies to the multiplier. If you put the initial amount and the multiplier in the brackets before taking a power, you also raise the initial amount.
  • Rounding the amount after each year changes the next year’s base and can shift the final answer.
revision.examTip: Count from period zero and round only the last result.

igcse-0580-exponential-growth-decay-deca.description: Apply a retained fraction repeatedly, distinguish the amount remaining from the amount lost and model depreciation.

sections.title: What part survives each period?
sections.label: Find the retained fraction
sections.intro: In an exponential decay model, the amount gets smaller by the same proportion in equal intervals. A later decline starts from the new, smaller amount.

blocks.html: For a loss of \(r\%\) per period, use \(m=1-\frac{r}{100}\), with \(0<m<1\). Halving means applying \(\frac12\) once per specified interval.

figure.alt: Five dots fall from sixty-four to four over four complete intervals.
figure.caption: The dots show repeated halving from \(64\) units.

blocks.title: Find the amount remaining after repeated loss
blocks.prompt: A pigment has initial mass \(800\) mg. It loses \(12\%\) of its remaining mass in each treatment. Find the exact mass remaining after \(2\) treatments.
blocks.solution:
One treatment retains \(88\%\). Use multiplier \(0.88\).

Apply it once per treatment. The remaining mass is \(800\times0.88^{2}=619.52\) mg.

\(800\times0.88^{2}=619.52\) mg remains.
blocks.hint: First find the amount retained in one stage, then repeat that multiplier.

blocks.html: For a loss of \(18\%\), a multiplier of \(0.18\) would keep only \(18\%\). The model needs the multiplier \(0.82\).

blocks.title: Halve the remaining amount at equal intervals
blocks.prompt: A light signal begins at \(452\) units. Under a model, half of the signal remains after every three hours. Find the signal strength after \(6\) hours.
blocks.solution:
There are \(\frac{6}{3}=2\) three-hour intervals.

Multiply by \(\frac12\) at the end of each interval.

\(452\left(\frac12\right)^{2}=113\) units.
blocks.hint: Read the period length. A half of the remaining amount is a multiplier of one half per period.

blocks.html: Find the length of the stated period before deciding which exponent to use.

sections.title: Am I finding the amount left or the amount lost?
sections.label: Read the required quantity
sections.intro: The model equation produces the amount remaining at a later time. Other questions use that result to ask for a difference or a percentage.

blocks.html: \(\text{amount lost}=\text{initial amount}-\text{amount remaining}\). The fraction still left after \(k\) periods is \(m^k\).

blocks.title: Find the amount lost in total
blocks.prompt: A pigment has initial mass \(1020\) mg. It loses \(15\%\) of its remaining mass in each treatment. How many milligrams are lost over \(2\) treatments? Give the exact amount.
blocks.solution:
One treatment retains \(85\%\). Use multiplier \(0.85\).

Apply it once per treatment. The remaining mass is \(1020\times0.85^{2}=736.95\) mg.

The total loss is \(1020-736.95=283.05\) mg.
blocks.hint: First find the amount retained in one stage, then repeat that multiplier.

retry.feedback: That is the amount remaining. Find how much is missing from the initial mass.

blocks.html: Multiplying the loss rate by the number of periods ignores the fact that each loss acts on a different amount.

blocks.title: Find what percentage of the original remains
blocks.prompt: A pigment has initial mass \(1980\) mg. It loses \(24\%\) of its remaining mass in each treatment. What percentage of the initial mass remains after \(3\) treatments? Give an exact percentage. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.solution:
One treatment retains \(76\%\). Use multiplier \(0.76\).

Apply it once per treatment. The remaining mass is \(1980\times0.76^{3}=869.17248\) mg.

The retained fraction is \(0.76^{3}=0.438976\), or \(43.8976\%\).
blocks.hint: First find the amount retained in one stage, then repeat that multiplier.

retry.feedback: That is the lost percentage. Give the percentage that remains.

blocks.html: Identify whether your answer needs a measurement unit or a percent sign.

sections.title: How do I use the same model for the value of an item?
sections.label: Model depreciation
sections.intro: An item that loses the same percentage of its current value each year follows an exponential depreciation model.

blocks.html: Multiply the original value by the annual retaining factor raised to the number of years. From a given model such as \(V_k=900(0.92)^k\), read an annual decrease of \(8\%\).

blocks.title: Model annual depreciation
blocks.prompt: A new cutting machine is valued at £13600. It loses \(22\%\) of its value each year. Estimate its value after \(2\) years, to the nearest pound.
blocks.solution:
It retains \(78\%\) of its value from one year to the next.

\(13600\times0.78^{2}\approx8274\) to the nearest pound.

The estimated value is £8274.
blocks.hint: Apply the retained fraction to the updated value each year.

blocks.html: The annual percentage loss can stay the same while the amount lost in pounds becomes smaller.

blocks.title: Read the percentage lost in one period
blocks.prompt: Signal strength is modelled by \(S(n)=380\times0.65^n\), where \(n\) counts elapsed hours. Find the percentage decrease per hour. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.solution:
After one hour \(65\%\) of the signal remains.

The other part is \(100-65=35\) percent of the signal at the start of that hour.
blocks.hint: Find how far below 1 the factor is, then convert that difference to a percentage.

retry.feedback: That is the percentage retained. The question asks for the percentage lost.

blocks.html: Take account of the question’s rounding instruction for a monetary forecast.

igcse-0580-exponential-growth-decay-reco.description: Use consecutive readings to recover a per-period multiplier, work back to an initial value and compare additive and exponential forecasts.

sections.title: How can a table reveal the multiplier?
sections.label: Compare consecutive readings
sections.intro: With equally spaced measurements, use a ratio to test for a constant factor. Use a difference to test for an additive model.

blocks.html: Divide one reading by the reading one period before it. Check the same ratio with another pair where data are supplied.

figure.alt: An additive path and a path with a constant ratio start at twenty and agree at thirty after one period. The path with a constant ratio is higher at periods two and three.
figure.caption: Both models start at \(20\). Adding \(10\) and multiplying by \(1.5\) agree after one step.

blocks.title: Recover the multiplier from paired readings
blocks.prompt:
The table gives three readings at equal intervals. Each reading is multiplied by the same number to get the next one. Find that multiplier.

Elapsed intervalsReading
\(0\)\(1000\)
\(1\)\(1120\)
\(2\)\(1254.4\)
blocks.solution:
Divide a later reading by the immediately preceding reading.

\(\frac{1120}{1000}=1.12\).

The next pair confirms the same factor. \(\frac{1254.4}{1120}=1.12\).
blocks.hint: Use consecutive values so the division gives exactly one interval’s multiplier.

retry.feedback: That is the fraction added or lost. The multiplier must produce the next whole reading.

blocks.html: A constant ratio may have increasing differences. Subtracting two readings gives a change in units and does not recover the multiplying factor.

blocks.title: Recover the multiplier from paired readings
blocks.prompt:
The table gives three readings at equal intervals. Each reading is multiplied by the same number to get the next one. Find that multiplier.

Elapsed intervalsReading
\(0\)\(2200\)
\(1\)\(1672\)
\(2\)\(1270.72\)
blocks.solution:
Divide a later reading by the immediately preceding reading.

\(\frac{1672}{2200}=0.76\).

The next pair confirms the same factor. \(\frac{1270.72}{1672}=0.76\).
blocks.hint: Use consecutive values so the division gives exactly one interval’s multiplier.

retry.feedback: That is the fraction added or lost. The multiplier must produce the next whole reading.

blocks.html: If two measurements are several periods apart, their ratio gives a combined factor. Use adjacent readings for a single-period factor.

sections.title: How do I recover the amount at time zero?
sections.label: Undo the entire power
sections.intro: A later reading has already had the multiplier applied once per completed period. The same equation can run backwards if the factor is positive.

blocks.html: \(A_k=A_0m^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A_0=\frac{A_k}{m^k}\). Check the recovered value with the original forward model.

blocks.title: Recover the initial value from a later reading
blocks.prompt: The model for a measure multiplies its value by \(1.18\) every hour. At the end of \(2\) hours its value is \(2158.22\) units. What was the value at the start, measured in units?
blocks.solution:
The original value was multiplied by \(1.18^{2}\).

Undo that factor. \(\frac{2158.22}{1.18^{2}}=1550\) units.

Substituting the original into the forward model recovers \(2158.22\) units.
blocks.hint: Divide the later reading by the multiplier raised to the number of elapsed hours.

retry.feedback: Dividing by the multiplier only once takes the reading back by one hour.

blocks.html: Dividing by \(m\) just once undoes one period, even when the question gives a value many periods later.

blocks.title: Recover the initial value from a later reading
blocks.prompt: The model for a measure multiplies its value by \(0.68\) every hour. At the end of \(3\) hours its value is \(864.688\) units. What was the value at the start, measured in units?
blocks.solution:
The original value was multiplied by \(0.68^{3}\).

Undo that factor. \(\frac{864.688}{0.68^{3}}=2750\) units.

Substituting the original into the forward model recovers \(864.688\) units.
blocks.hint: Divide the later reading by the multiplier raised to the number of elapsed hours.

retry.feedback: Dividing by the multiplier only once takes the reading back by one hour.

blocks.html: Write the complete power in the denominator or use brackets if entering it on a calculator.

sections.title: How are rate, factor and fixed change different?
sections.label: Interpret and compare predictions
sections.intro: An exponential predictor keeps its multiplier. An additive predictor keeps its change in units. You can compare two results at the same time.

blocks.html: Convert factor to rate by comparing it with 1. For a factor above 1, the extra part is growth. For a factor below 1, the missing part is decay.

blocks.title: Infer a rate from two consecutive readings
blocks.prompt: Under an exponential model, a reading is \(1212.96\) at the end of hour \(2\) and \(921.8496\) at the end of hour \(3\). Find the percentage decrease per hour. Enter the number before the percent sign.
blocks.solution:
Divide the later reading by the earlier one to find one hour’s multiplier.

\(\frac{921.8496}{1212.96}=0.76\).

Its difference from 1 gives the fractional change. The decrease is \(24\%\).
blocks.hint: Separate the multiplier from the percentage change. The ratio is the full multiplier.

retry.feedback: That is the later amount as a percentage of the earlier one. Find the change from 100 percent.

blocks.html: Two models can agree at the first step and then separate. Matching the first change does not make the forecasts identical.

blocks.title: Compare a fixed increase with a proportional one
blocks.prompt: Two forecasts start at \(475\) units. Forecast A adds \(190\) units every month. Forecast B grows by \(40\%\) each month. How many units higher is forecast B after \(2\) months? Give the exact difference.
blocks.solution:
The additive model increases by the same amount every month. \(475+2\times190=855\).

The other model uses the same multiplier each month. \(475\times1.4^{2}=931\).

The difference is \(931-855=76\) units.
blocks.hint: The first forecast needs multiplication of the fixed increase by the time. The second uses a power of the multiplier.

retry.feedback: The gains match after the first month. Later gains in the exponential model use a higher base.

blocks.html: Use the same elapsed period in both models and compare their final amounts with the same unit.

revision.body:
Methods

MethodWhat to do
Compare consecutive readingsDivide one reading by the reading one period before it. Check the same ratio with another pair where data are supplied.
Undo the entire power\(A_k=A_0m^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A_0=\frac{A_k}{m^k}\). Check the recovered value with the original forward model.
Interpret and compare predictionsConvert factor to rate by comparing it with 1. For a factor above 1, the extra part is growth. For a factor below 1, the missing part is decay.

Worked line

\(\frac{405}{270}=1.5\)

Check yourself

A model returns \(172.8\) at the end of three periods and has multiplier \(1.2\). Find its initial value.

Answer \(100\)
revision.checks:
• A constant ratio may have increasing differences. Subtracting two readings gives a change in units and does not recover the multiplying factor.
  • Dividing by \(m\) just once undoes one period, even when the question gives a value many periods later.
  • Two models can agree at the first step and then separate. Matching the first change does not make the forecasts identical.
revision.examTip: For a per-period factor, compare readings one period apart.

igcse-0580-exponential-growth-decay-thre.description: Check successive whole periods and use the exact inequality to find the first time a growth or decay target is met.

sections.title: When does a growing amount first reach a target?
sections.label: Check consecutive periods
sections.intro: Write down the starting amount, factor and comparison. Evaluate the model at successive whole periods until the condition first holds.

blocks.html: A growth model with factor above 1 is increasing. If the current reading passes the target and the preceding reading fails, this is the first successful period.

figure.alt: A growing sequence has values forty, sixty, ninety and one hundred and thirty-five. The target is one hundred, so the third interval is the first one above it.
figure.caption: The end-of-period values \(90\) and \(135\) lie on different sides of the target \(100\).

blocks.title: Find the first whole-period threshold
blocks.prompt: A reading starts at \(850\) units. In the model it rises by \(15\%\) each day. Find the first whole number of days after which the reading is strictly above \(1210\) units.
blocks.solution:
Each interval multiplies the reading by \(1.15\). Work forwards until the condition is first true.

Completed intervalsReadingCompare with target
\(2\)\(1124.125\)\(1124.125\le1210\)
\(3\)\(1292.74375\)\(1292.74375>1210\)

So the first possible time is \(3\) days.
blocks.hint: List successive values. Check both the first value that works and the value one period before it.

retry.feedback: One interval earlier does not meet the exact condition. Check whether the boundary includes equality.

blocks.html: Showing only a successful value leaves open whether an earlier value already worked.

blocks.title: Find the first whole-period threshold

blocks.hint: List successive values. Check both the first value that works and the value one period before it.

retry.feedback: One interval earlier does not meet the exact condition. Check whether the boundary includes equality.

blocks.html: Give both the first successful value and the one just before it when asked to justify the first period.

sections.title: When does a falling amount first go low enough?
sections.label: Compare precisely at the boundary
sections.intro: For a falling amount, the readings are decreasing. A lower limit may use an inclusive comparison or a strict one.

blocks.html: ‘At most’ allows equality and uses \(\le\). ‘Strictly below’ excludes equality and uses \(<\). Use unrounded model values near a boundary.

blocks.html: A value equal to the cutoff is the first successful one only when the instruction includes equality.

sections.title: What if the period is different from the requested unit?
sections.label: Convert the winning interval
sections.intro: Sometimes a model factor applies per week or every three hours. Successive model values are checked only at the specified completed intervals.

blocks.html: First find the number of full intervals. Multiply the winning interval count by the number of days, weeks or hours in one interval, as requested.
